name: Southwestern Dinka
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Nebel 1948 Dinka Grammar (Rek-Malual) read in full text on archive.org (dinkagrammara.nebel): no explicit word-stress rule; 'accent' used only for grammatical prominence (pos/neg verbs, cases)

new_statements.quote: Described in terms of the elements distributed in it and the features which characterize it, the phonological word is the unit of stress placement in the phonological hierarchy. Each phonological word has one and only one stress. The factors that condition stress have not been studied and, as mentioned, are not the concern of this discussion. It is clear, however, that stress is neither contrastive nor used at all in connection with semantic emphasis in Dinka. The final margin of the phonological word is characterized by potential pause. The phonological word is the level of distribution of the syllable: one syllable is stressed in each word.
new_statements.citation: Malou, Job. 1988. Dinka Vowel System. Summer Institute of Linguistics Publications in Linguistics 82. Dallas: Summer Institute of Linguistics and The University of Texas at Arlington.
new_statements.locator: ch. 2 'An overview of Dinka phonological structure', sec. 2.2 'The Phonological Word', p. 9 (examples (5) on p. 10); PDF pages 20-21 of the ERIC fiche scan
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dinka is a tone language (every syllable carries one tone, sec. 2.3; four tonemes per Remijsen & Ladd 2008 for Luanyjang) whose stems are almost all monosyllabic. Malou states that each phonological word (a unit bounded by potential pause, often host+clitic or a short phrase) bears exactly one non-contrastive stress, but explicitly declines to state what determines its position. His marked examples put the stress on the lexical head/root of the unit ('mony dit 'old man', 'ɣok lṳac 'pregnant cows', 'muoc meth 'give the child', but aca 'yat 'I have taken it' with stress on the verb root after the auxiliary clitic), i.e. consistent with root/head stress, though the author does not say so. The SW-specific modern descriptions (Remijsen & Manyang 2009: 120; Remijsen & Ladd 2008) give no stress rule at all: one toneme per morpheme, associated with the rightmost (usually only) syllable, with a predictable non-distinctive high pitch on the penult of disyllables; Gilley's (2003) 'stress' feature is a re-labelling of the morphological short vowel grade and found no acoustic support in Luanyjang (Remijsen & Gilley 2008, as reported in JIPA fn. 5).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Malou says the conditioning factors are unstudied. Remijsen & Manyang note polysyllables are limited to /aCVC/ nouns, loans and compounds.
new_statements.domain_note: Malou's domain is the 'phonological word' = pause-bounded unit larger than the grammatical word (his examples are two-word phrases and aux+verb groups); statement is for Dinka as a whole (four varieties incl. Western/Rek), from the author's own speech, variety not stated on the pages read. Citation-form monosyllables trivially carry the stress ('lec).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted stress statement (Malou 1988) is for Dinka as a whole (macro-language, glottocode dink1262), written by a native speaker whose own variety is not stated on the pages read; he lists 'Western, which is Rek based' among the four varieties his analysis is meant to cover. The Southwestern-specific modern descriptions are of Luanyjang (Luac) Dinka, Rek cluster, which Remijsen & Manyang 2009 place in South-Western Dinka = sout2832; those describe tone only and give no stress rule. Nebel 1948 (Rek-Malual, sout2832 proper) is silent on word stress. Remijsen 2013 (also saved) is Bor = Southeastern Dinka (sout2836) and should not be used for this key.

sources.locator: ch. 2 'An overview of Dinka phonological structure', sec. 2.2 'The Phonological Word', p. 9 (examples (5) on p. 10); PDF pages 20-21 of the ERIC fiche scan
sources.note: Pan-Dinka description by a native speaker (covers 'four major varieties' incl. 'Western, which is Rek based', p.1-2). Sec. 2.2 p.9-10: phonological word is the unit of stress placement; exactly one stress per phonological word; conditioning factors 'have not been studied'; stress not contrastive; examples (5) with stress marks: aca 'yat 'I have taken it', 'muoc meth 'give the child', 'mony dit 'old man', 'ɣok lṳac 'pregnant cows', 'lec 'teeth'. Sec. 2.3: syllable is the unit of tone placement, every syllable carries one tone.

sources.note: SW Dinka proper. Sound chapter treats vowels, 'breathed' vowels and consonants only; no word-stress or tone placement rule. 'Accent(uated)' is used only for grammatical prominence (positive verb 'more accentuated' than negative; object-case vowel lengthening 'should be stressed in speaking'; readers vs object distinguished 'only by the accent'). Confirms the earlier scan's NO-SOURCE-FOUND note for this work.

sources.citation: Remijsen, Bert & Caguor Adong Manyang. 2009. Luanyjang Dinka. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 39(1): 113-124. doi:10.1017/S0025100308003605 (publisher OA PDF)
sources.note: Luanyjang = Luac, Rek cluster (SW Dinka). No word-stress placement rule. Tone section p.120: 'There are four distinctive tone patterns (tonemes) - Low, High, Rise, and Fall. Each morpheme carries one, irrespective of its number of syllables. This toneme associates with the rightmost syllable, which is usually the only syllable. In polysyllabic words, the penultimate syllable may have high pitch. This high pitch is not distinctive.' sources.citation: Remijsen, Bert & D. Robert Ladd. 2008. The tone system of the Luanyjang dialect of Dinka. Journal of African Languages and Linguistics 29(2): 173-213. doi:10.1515/JALL.2008.009 (Edinburgh postprint via CORE)
sources.note: No mention of word stress at all (the word 'stress/accent' appears only in reference titles). Sec. 2.3 and 4.1: four tonemes, one per morpheme regardless of syllable count, Association Rule links the toneme to the rightmost syllable of the morpheme; TBU = syllable; penult of /aCVC/ disyllables gets a predictable H.
